chapter_theme: Energetic effort (தாளாண்மை): it makes a person, as a twig hardens into an elephant post, supports kin and an ageing father, and is what lineage really consists of. Manliness is persisting when things fail, and food won by one's own effort tastes better than a patron's feast.
structure_note: Mudaliar's commentary is not aligned for 191 to 195, so for those quatrains only Shanmuganar and Pope are available.

191.reading: Like the green crop below a tank that does not hold back its water, kin live by what their relative gives and rest easy; can failure come to the energetic, who move as quickly as the eyes of women in the sword dance?
191.nuance: Pope reads the first half in reverse: kin who live on handouts die off like crops under a tank that holds too little water. The Tamil supports Shanmuganar's 'rest' (துஞ்சுப) at least as well, so the verse probably praises the energetic as the one who feeds the family.

positions.position: The other kin live without hardship on what the energetic one gives.

192.reading: A twig that swayed by the path, once its core has hardened, becomes a post to tether an elephant; life is like that too, if a person makes himself without slackening.
192.nuance: Shanmuganar reads தாழ்வின்றி as not letting oneself sink; Pope as 'unfailing'. Either way the self is something made over time.

193.reading: A mighty tiger that finds no meat one day will catch and eat even a small frog; so do not think your knowledge fits you only for lowly work: through skill, higher work will come in that very place.
193.nuance: Pope titles it 'Stoop to conquer'. Shanmuganar reads the advice as taking the humble job that is available, since better skilled work may follow.

194.reading: Manliness is standing firm in the way one has undertaken even when the thing does not succeed; lord of the cool seashore groves, when things succeed by themselves, don't even women manage to live?
194.nuance: The taunt assumes that women cannot persist through failure. The point is that persistence, not success, is the measure of effort.

195.reading: 'Good caste' and 'bad caste' are only words with nothing behind them; not long-famous wealth but austerity, learning and effort are what make a lineage.
195.nuance: A strong claim from a Jain text that questions birth rank. Shanmuganar takes ஒண்பொருள் ஒன்றோ as asking whether fine wealth alone suffices; Pope reads it as 'not even by possessions'.

196.reading: The perceptive keep their plans to themselves until the work is done and do not voice their drive; the world lies under the sign of those bright ones who read others' drive from their features.
196.nuance: Mudaliar takes the first ஊக்கம் as one's own effort and the second as the stirring in others' minds, so the verse pairs concealment with insight. He also records a reading in which the world serves at their nod.

197.reading: When termites have eaten the banyan, its aerial roots stand as pillars and hold it up; so when weakness shows in a father, the son he begot covers it and it disappears.
197.nuance: Mudaliar notes that மதலை, the prop, also means a son, so the image and the claim share a word.

198.reading: Those with the strength of a lion, whose sharp claws and mighty paws wound an elephant's spotted face, would sooner die in want and low estate at home than do anything that brings disgrace.
198.nuance: Mudaliar reads மானம் here as dishonour (அவமானம்) and maps the lion's claws onto keen intelligence and resourceful effort.

199.reading: As the cane flower on its thick stalk, with its mane of filaments, loses its honeyed scent, what is birth in a lofty family worth without the great manliness that engraves one's name?

200.reading: The base fill themselves on rice and fried dishes that the great Mutharaiyar give with delight; but for those who do not even know the names of such dishes, water won by their own eager effort becomes nectar.
200.nuance: Pope makes the Mutharaiyar 'lords of the triple lands', one of the readings Mudaliar reports. The verse brands even the guests of a generous patron as base for living on another's food.

positions.position: The Mutharaiyar were best taken as a generous patron of the poet's own time.

links.note: 615 calls the one who prefers work to pleasure a pillar who wipes away his kin's troubles. On Shanmuganar's reading of 191, kin rest easy on what the energetic one provides.
611 says effort brings the greatness the task requires; 192 shows it as a twig hardening into a post strong enough for an elephant.
618 says bad fortune is no disgrace but failing to work is; 193 tells the knowledgeable not to scorn humble work when fortune is thin.
198 says the lion-hearted would die rather than do anything disgraceful; 193 says even the tiger eats a frog when hungry. Read together, humble work is not disgrace, and dishonourable deeds are.
619 says effort pays its wage even when fate denies the goal; 194 makes persistence through failure the very definition of manliness.
Both begin from success or failure (இசையும் எனினும் இசையாதெனினும் in 152, இசையாதெனினும் in 194) and judge a person by how they act regardless of outcome.
972: birth is alike for all beings, and distinction differs by the work done. 195 says good and bad caste are mere words and lineage is made by austerity, learning and effort.

951 says integrity and shame exist together naturally only in the well-born. 195 says good and bad lineage are words without substance. Both concern whether birth carries real moral qualities, and they answer opposite ways unless 951's இற்பிறந்தார் is read as a lineage made by conduct, as 195 defines it.

On Shanmuganar's reading of 179, the worthy are formed by the family they are born into, as paddy by its soil; 195 says good and bad lineage are only words. On Mudaliar's reading of குலம் in 179 as one's company, there is no conflict.
663 says true manliness lets a deed be known only when finished, since revealing it midway brings grief; 196 says the perceptive keep their plans to themselves until the work is done.
701 calls one who reads what is unsaid an ornament to the world; 196 says the world is under the sign of those who read others' drive from their features.
Both picture a structure eaten at the base and propped up. In 1030 a family whose foot is cut by trouble falls if no good person props it; in 197 the son props the decaying father like banyan roots.
70 says a son repays his father by making people wonder what penance the father did. 197 gives a more practical repayment: covering the father's weakness when he falters.
656: even seeing one's mother starve, do not do what the worthy condemn. 198: even dying in want at home, the strong do not do what brings disgrace.
Both set death against dishonour: 969's yak dies when it loses its hair, 198's lion-hearted would die in want rather than be disgraced.
601 says the lamp of lineage dies when sloth covers it; 199 says high birth is worth nothing without great manliness, like a flower that has lost its scent.
Nearly the same claim: 1065 says even watery gruel got by one's own effort (தாள்தந்தது) is the sweetest food, and 200 says water won by one's own effort (தாளாண்மை) becomes nectar.

In 200 the Mutharaiyar are patrons whose feasts the base enjoy; in 296 the poor who never go begging to the rich are themselves called Mutharaiyar. The patron's name moves from giver to the self-reliant.

source_issues: 191-195: Mudaliar's commentary is not aligned for any of these quatrains.
199: Tamil has a corrupted character in உளையலா஢, which Mudaliar's gloss shows is அலரி.
